questions.question: Why can one proxied request consume more than one NGINX worker connection slot?
options: Every request creates a second worker process
The worker may own both the downstream client socket and an upstream socket
The cache key opens a listening socket
TLS always uses four upstream connections
questions.explanation: A proxied request commonly occupies a downstream connection and an upstream connection. Long-lived requests, keep-alive, retries, and protocols change how long those slots remain active.

questions.question: Traffic is 50,000 requests per second with an 88% edge-cache hit rate. How many requests per second reach the origin before retries?
questions.explanation: The miss rate is 12%, so 50,000 x 0.12 = 6,000 origin requests per second.

questions.question: When is least-connections routing more informative than round robin?
options: When every request has identical duration and servers are idle
When request durations vary and active connections provide a useful load signal
When the application requires a durable transaction log
When no upstream servers exist
questions.explanation: Least connections can account for uneven request duration by steering new work away from servers with more active connections, though connection count is still only a proxy for actual load.

questions.question: Why is retrying a timed-out POST dangerous without an application idempotency contract?
options: POST responses cannot contain headers
The first attempt may have committed even though its response did not arrive
NGINX cannot connect to more than one upstream
The retry always becomes a GET
questions.explanation: A timeout makes the final result unknown. Repeating a state-changing request can create another durable effect unless a stable operation ID converges on the original outcome.

questions.question: Which pair most directly contains a hot-key cache-expiry stampede?
options: A larger access log and a longer URL
Cache-fill locking and an explicit stale-serving policy
IP hash and client cookies
More forwarding headers and fewer cache keys
questions.explanation: A cache lock elects a refresh owner, while permitted stale serving can keep other callers off the origin during update or error. Both need bounded freshness and timeout rules.

questions.question: When may NGINX safely treat X-Forwarded-For as authoritative client identity?
options: Whenever any internet client sends it
Only after a trusted edge strips untrusted values and accepts metadata from known proxy ranges
Only when the request is a POST
Whenever the cache returns a hit
questions.explanation: Forwarding metadata is trustworthy only across an explicit network trust boundary. Otherwise a client can forge the address used by policy and audit systems.

questions.question: What must an operator account for during a graceful NGINX reload?
options: All established connections are always terminated immediately
Old and new worker generations can overlap while long-lived connections drain
The cache is automatically purged
Every upstream is marked down
questions.explanation: New workers accept traffic with the new configuration while old workers finish existing connections. Resource use and policy overlap must remain observable until the old generation exits.
